To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the frequency of germlin BRCA1 mutations is relatively high in the population of Yugoslav families with breast and breast/ ovarian cancer and that there is no evidence for population specific founder mutations.
the frequency of BRCA1 mutations in Yugoslav breast cancer families is high (33%) and that there is a possible common founder for the most common BRCA1 mutation in the population (185delAG).
we identified 3 different recurrent BRCA 1 mutations in 4 of the 12 families ( 33%) and that the relatively high frequency of BRCA1 mutations confirms the important role in disease predisposition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of BRCA1/2 mutations in families with breast cancer in Serbia.
the identification of the most frequent germline BRAC1 and BRCA 2 mutations in the population of Yugoslavia and the analysis of the founder effect in the region.
the genetic basis of breast and ovarian cancer predisposition in a population from the Balkan region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

BRCA1 is the most common breast cancer gene in the Yugoslav breast cancer population, and that the majority of BRCA1 mutations found in the population are not unique, but rather recurrent, suggesting the possibility of common founder effects.
the prevalence of BRCA1 mutations in the Yugoslavian breast/ovarian families is comparable to that of other populations.
BRCA1 mutations are frequent in the Yugoslav breast/ ovarian cancer families, but that BRCA2 is probably not a major contributor in the pathogenesis of this type of cancer in the region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that in the region of former Yugoslavia, the frequency of germlin BRCA1 mutations is high, while BRCA2 mutations are rare.
BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 germline mutations account for approximately 50% of breast/ovarian familial cancer in this population.
the BRCA1 gene is the most important gene involved in breast/ovarian cancers in the Yugoslav region, and that it is likely that the BRCA2 gene is also involved in the etiology of this disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the frequency of the BRCA1 5382insc mutation in the Yugoslav female breast cancer population is 2% which is similar to that in the general European population.
the genetic background of breast/ovarian cancers is complex and the role of BRCA2 in the etiology of these tumors should not be underestimated.
we have shown that the frequency of BRCA1 mutation in our population is higher than the average in the European population.
